hook.title: Same coffee. Different choice.
hook.scenario: Two coffee shops sell the same drink. One costs less; the other is closer and has a quiet seat. Why might you choose the second?
options: The drink is the whole story.
hook.explanation: Nice observation: price is only one cost. Convenience and a useful experience can add value for a particular customer.

model.title: Build a strategy, one decision at a time
model.intro: Select a glowing node. Answer its question to open the next connection. This compact introduction combines decisions and outcomes; Module 3 provides the full Figure 1-1 learning map.

nodes.label: Market analysis
nodes.explanation: Investigate customers, your company, competitors, and market conditions. This gives you evidence for the next decisions.
nodes.example: A hypothetical Starbucks team compares what commuters need with what nearby cafés offer.

quiz.prompt: Before choosing an audience, what should you investigate?
quiz.explanation: Market analysis examines the market before committing to a solution.

nodes.label: Segmentation
nodes.explanation: Identify different sets of needs and group people with similar needs. Describe those groups so you can understand and reach them.
nodes.example: An original café scenario groups quiet-study seekers separately from quick-pickup commuters.

options: Everyone born in the same month
People needing a quiet place to study
quiz.explanation: The group shares a relevant problem the offering could solve.

nodes.label: Target selection
nodes.explanation: Evaluate which segment is attractive and feasible to serve. Fit matters: your resources must support the value you promise.
nodes.example: A hypothetical small café chooses study sessions because it has seats and reliable Wi-Fi.

quiz.prompt: Your café has six seats. Which question matters before targeting all-day study groups?
options: Can our space support their needs profitably?
quiz.explanation: A target must fit your capabilities as well as its needs and attractiveness.

nodes.label: Marketing mix
nodes.explanation: Coordinate the offering, price, communication, distribution, and service. Together they should deliver value to the chosen customers.
nodes.example: In an invented Shopee purchase, delivery, product information, price, and service all shape the offer.

quiz.prompt: Which plan supports a quick-pickup audience?
options: A long queue with a convenience slogan
Pre-ordering plus a reliable pickup process
A new slogan with no service change
quiz.explanation: The actual experience must support the promised benefit.

nodes.label: Decisions & outcomes
nodes.explanation: Observe what happens for consumers, the firm, and society. Use that evidence to revisit assumptions instead of assuming the strategy worked.
nodes.example: An original café scenario checks repeat visits, customer complaints, and cup disposal—not just initial sales.

quiz.prompt: Which outcome would a checkout-only view miss?
options: Use, disposal, and later customer experience
quiz.explanation: Consumer behavior extends beyond acquisition and includes broader consequences.

concepts.definition: How people select, acquire, use, and dispose of offerings to meet needs, including consequences for people and society.
concepts.analogy: Think of the whole movie, not just the checkout scene.
concepts.analogyLimit: Real decisions can loop or overlap rather than follow a script.
concepts.example: Hypothetical IKEA shopper: compare desks, buy one, use it, then donate it.
concepts.mistake: Only the person paying and the moment of purchase matter.
concepts.question: Why should a marketer investigate what happens after purchase?
concepts.answer: Use, evaluation, and disposal shape later decisions and affect consumers and society.
concepts.hint: Think about use, evaluation, and disposal.
concepts.vi: Hành vi người tiêu dùng gồm chọn, mua, sử dụng và thải bỏ; không chỉ là lúc thanh toán.

activity.prompt: A customer donates an old desk. Is this consumer behavior?
options: Yes: disposal is part of consumption
activity.explanation: Disposal is included even when nothing new is bought.

concepts.quote: select, secure, use, and dispose of products, services, experiences, or ideas

concepts.definition: Perceived benefits minus all the costs of getting those benefits.
concepts.analogy: A backpack has rewards inside—and weight you must carry.
concepts.analogyLimit: Value is perceived, not a precise score measured by this analogy.
concepts.example: Hypothetical café choice: a higher price can be worthwhile if it saves a long walk.
concepts.mistake: The cheapest price always means the greatest value.
concepts.question: How could a more expensive café provide greater customer value?
concepts.answer: Benefits such as a useful space or lower time and effort costs may outweigh the higher price for that customer.
concepts.hint: Include time, effort, and benefits—not only price.
concepts.vi: Giá trị khách hàng là lợi ích cảm nhận trừ toàn bộ chi phí, kể cả thời gian và công sức.

activity.prompt: Which cost can remain even when the drink is free?
activity.explanation: Waiting consumes time. A zero price does not remove every customer cost.

concepts.quote: Customer value is the difference between all the benefits

concepts.definition: Group customers with similar product-related needs, then describe and select groups to serve.
concepts.analogy: Sort study playlists by purpose before choosing who each one helps.
concepts.analogyLimit: People can share several needs; segments are not permanent boxes.
concepts.example: Original café scenario: quiet-study customers and rush-hour commuters need different experiences.
concepts.mistake: Dividing people by age alone finishes segmentation.
concepts.question: Name the four segmentation steps and explain why needs come first.
concepts.answer: Identify need sets; group customers with similar needs; describe each group; select attractive groups the business can serve. Needs identify the value to provide.
concepts.vi: Phân khúc: xác định nhu cầu → nhóm khách có nhu cầu giống nhau → mô tả nhóm → chọn nhóm phù hợp.

activity.prompt: Which step comes before describing a segment?
activity.explanation: Find the shared needs and groups before describing who is in them.

concepts.quote: focusing first on needs and then on consumer characteristics associated with those needs

case.title: Your café. Three decisions.
case.context: Campus Cup is a fictional café near a university. You have reliable Wi-Fi, twelve seats, and a limited budget. Build an offer that fits.

options: Students who need a quiet 60-minute study break
rounds.explanation: A shared usage need gives you a clearer basis for an offer than an extremely broad or decorative grouping.

options: Quiet seating, clear seat availability, and dependable Wi-Fi
A large discount with no seating plan
rounds.explanation: Align the marketing mix with the need. A promise your capacity cannot support creates a mismatch.

rounds.prompt: What should you learn after opening?
options: Only how many people paid today
Whether the space meets needs, repeat visits occur, and waste is handled
rounds.explanation: Evaluate use, later experiences, and consequences alongside sales. This gives evidence to improve the strategy.

sort.title: Pack the value backpack
sort.description: Drag each item to Benefits or Costs. Or select an item, then select a category.

items.label: Enjoyable taste
items.explanation: Taste can add a benefit the customer values.

items.label: Reliable Wi-Fi
items.explanation: A useful service can add a benefit in a study context.

items.label: Time in a queue
items.explanation: Time is a cost even when the selling price is low.

items.label: Delivery fee
items.explanation: A fee adds to the monetary costs of the offer.

sequence.title: Build a needs-first segment
sequence.description: Drag the steps into order, or use the up and down buttons.
sequence.explanation: Start with the value people need, organize similar needs, describe the groups, then select whom you can serve.

match.title: Connect the idea
match.description: Match each term to its meaning. Drag a term onto a definition, or select one of each.

mistake.title: Spot the costly assumption
mistake.prompt: “Our drink is cheapest, so every customer gets the most value.” What is the mistake?
options: It ignores benefits and non-price costs
It checks whether people need the offer
mistake.explanation: A low price can be outweighed by time, effort, or missing benefits. Compare total value for the target customer.

flash.title: Flashcard sprint
flash.description: Recall the term before revealing it. Optional elapsed-time mode adds a combo, not a deadline.

cards.prompt: The process includes use and disposal, not just buying.
First step before grouping and describing customers.
